Using the Bestiary

Dry clicking answers the heroes' footsteps. Scraps tied to a ruined wall mark a safe path through the debris. Coins beneath a bridge have been sorted with surprising care. Before a creature attacks, it can already tell the players something about the place they have entered.

The bestiary gives you creatures to portray and complete cards to run. Use the signs, purpose and counterplay alongside the statistics. A creature is more useful when you know why it is here and what might make it leave.

Read from the top down

Every creature's name includes its current CV. Beneath a short description, find its six attributes, HP, Speed, Size, Armor DR, Evasion, Threat and Stability on the left, with weaknesses, resistances and immunities on the right. Unique actions come next, with defense, damage type and complete outcomes in the table. Details below describe the action, its targets and any remaining limits. The final section collects healing, senses, signs, motives and encounter guidance.

FieldUse during play
AttributesThe creature's printed values when a roll uses them. PC defense against it still uses the PC's named attribute.
HPIts immediate endurance. Ordinary creatures die at 0 unless an explicit exception applies.
SpeedIts available movement, subject to terrain and its printed movement modes.
SizeOccupied footprint. Size 2 occupies 2 × 2 squares; it does not automatically grant reach or Stability.
Armor DRPhysical resistance, always shown even at 0. An asterisk points to additional resistance types below.
EvasionBoons or Banes applied to player attacks against it.
ThreatBoons or Banes applied to player defenses against its attacks, unless an attack states an exception.
StabilityForced movement consumed by its resistance to displacement; highest grant, maximum 3.
WeaknessesNumerical damage weaknesses or explicit special vulnerabilities. Read the details.
ResistancesDamage types and reductions. The Physical entry repeats Armor DR; never add them together.
ImmunitiesOnly the printed immunities apply. Category names grant none by themselves.

0 under Evasion or Threat means no modifier from that field. “1 Bane” means one Bane through the ordinary dice procedure, not minus one to a total.

Choose the moment to react

A creature’s distinctive Reaction competes with its opportunity attack for the same single Reaction. A duelist may save it to turn a blade, a guardian to cover a companion, or a dragon to sweep a damaging attacker away. Read the trigger before the dice: interference comes before the roll, protection before the damage, and retaliation after the incoming attack resolves. A creature that dies or loses the required capability cannot retaliate.

Several named movement Maneuvers trade distance for avoiding one chosen enemy’s opportunity attack. Other enemies still threaten the route. Converting the Maneuver into a full movement allowance remains useful when distance alone matters. Abilities belong only to the creatures that print them; a family name grants none. A summoned profile has its own permitted Maneuvers and no independent Reactions.

A Goblin Scrapper at the table

The @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.da-rules.JournalEntry.4711412dc1b011a9.JournalEntryPage.d65ecdabb2fc906b]{Goblin Scrapper} has CV 8, HP 8, Speed 7, Size 1, Armor DR 0, Evasion 1 Bane, Threat 0 and Stability 0. Its Scrap knife requires Agility defense and deals 5/3/2 physical damage for Weak/Standard/Strong player defense.

A hero attacking it suffers 1 Bane from Evasion. If the goblin has used Defend, that adds another Bane until its stated expiry. An applicable Boon cancels one; apply the usual net cap. The goblin does not roll to dodge the attack.

When the goblin uses Scrap knife, its target rolls Agility. On Standard defense, the attack deals 3 physical damage before resistance. A hero with Physical resistance 2 takes 1. On Strong defense, the attack deals 2 before resistance and still deals the minimum 1 total damage. The goblin's Agility +2 does not get added to that player's defense roll or to the knife's damage.

Slip the Rush lets the goblin spend its Reaction after a visible enemy ends voluntary movement adjacent to it, moving 1 square without an opportunity from that enemy. Other enemies still threaten the route. Spending it means the goblin has no Reaction left for an opportunity attack until its normal refresh.

On its turn, the goblin can use its Main Action for an attack and its Maneuver for Roll Away, moving up to two squares in a straight line without provoking. Roll Away still obeys terrain and occupied-square restrictions. Choosing it means the goblin did not spend that same Maneuver on Defend. Its purpose is to protect a salvage claim; a useful tool or a recognized claim may matter more to it than a fight.

Read complete outcomes

The DA card's damage columns read Weak defense / Standard defense / Strong defense. Weak is dangerous for the defending hero. Each slash separates a complete outcome, including conditions and movement. Do not combine the riders from several columns or apply a Strong-defense rider to every result.

A line such as “6 + Bleeding 2 / 4 + Bleeding 1 / 3” means exactly those three alternatives. The damage type has its own table column; range and target appear in the action's details. A zero-damage condition result remains a condition result; the minimum-damage rule does not invent damage for an effect that deals none.

Healing and other nonattack actions use their own details rather than this damage legend. A healing action's Strong result is beneficial when healing an eligible ally. When the same ability harms a healing-harmed target, use its printed harmful procedure and defense outcomes.

Actions are choices

A creature has the normal Main Action, Maneuver, Reaction and movement. Several attacks give options. A claw, bite and breath weapon do not all occur on one Main Action unless a printed action explicitly combines them.

Read a maneuver before deciding it fits. Check range, path, endpoint, duration and usage limits. Use the printed Reaction trigger and cost. Opportunity attacks use Basic Melee and occur before the provoking action; the original action continues if its actor is still capable. The specialty attack is not an opportunity substitute.

Mark expiring effects where you can see them. Defend adds a temporary Bane to player attacks against that creature; it does not change permanent Evasion. A shield's hunker consumes a Reaction; defense rolls do not.

Universal actions

Creature cards list their unique actions. The following universal choices are available when the creature is capable of performing them; they are not repeated on each card.

ActionUse
Basic Melee — Main ActionAttack one adjacent creature. Agility defense; physical damage; printed Threat applies. No specialty riders.
Defend — ManeuverAdd 1 Bane to player attacks against the creature until the start of its next turn. Combines with Evasion through normal Boon/Bane rules; repeated Defend does not stack.
Opportunity Attack — ReactionBasic Melee against the provoking creature, before its action resolves. That action continues if its actor remains capable.

Basic Melee uses the following existing creature damage profiles. Read each as Weak / Standard / Strong player defense. This reference also supplies the attack used for opportunity attacks; do not substitute a specialty attack.

CreaturesBasic Melee damage
Cave Bat; Raven2/1/1
Adder; Skeleton Archer; Clockwork Scout; Emberling; Goblin Scrapper; Grave Wisp; Hearth Brownie; Hedge Sprite; Kobold Trapkeeper; Lantern Spirit; Rill Sprite; Trail Hound4/2/1
All other creatures in this bestiary5/3/2

Damage defenses in order

For each damage component, add its applicable numerical weakness, then subtract its matching resistance. Use the highest value of a given type rather than adding several sources; the normal cap is 3. Do not add a weakness for a damage type the event never included. Apply minimum 1 damage to the whole damaging event after its components have been reduced.

> Example: mixed damage. An event deals 4 Physical and 1 Fire. Fire Weakness 2 > changes the Fire component to 3. Physical resistance 2 and Fire resistance 1 > leave 2 Physical plus 2 Fire, for 4 total. Armor DR and Physical resistance are > the same value, not two reductions.

A special vulnerability follows its own wording. Fire stops the Bridge Troll's Knit Flesh for the stated interval; it does not automatically add Fire damage. The troll recovers HP only while above 0 and cannot regenerate from death.

Forced movement and Stability

All actors start at Stability 0 unless an explicit trait, ability or item says otherwise. On creature cards, Heavy Frame identifies a permanent grant. A large footprint by itself grants none. Use the highest applicable source, maximum 3.

Deduct the initial target's Stability once before forced movement. Terrain then consumes movement by square: normal 1, difficult 2. Any positive remaining budget can enter the last square and stop even if its cost exceeds that budget.

When the moving creature or group strikes another movable creature, resolve collision damage from the movement remaining at contact. Apply applicable damage resistance, then deduct the new member's Stability. Continue as one group if movement remains. Never charge the same member's Stability twice during that movement.

> Example: a collision chain. Push 5 meets Stability 1, leaving 4. The target > crosses one normal square, leaving 3, then collides with a Stability-2 creature. > Both receive 3 collision damage before applicable resistance. Deduct the new > member's Stability 2, leaving 1 for further group movement.

A hard obstruction stops the group and adds 1 to the remaining-budget collision damage. Every member takes the applicable damage. Finish in separate legal spaces; if everyone cannot fit, stop at the last position where they can. You choose the arrangement without granting extra forward movement or passage through walls. The original mover bounces one square opposite afterward where possible.

Stability does not resist Prone, grapples, conditions or damage. If Stability prevents a push, the attack's other effects still occur.

Play purpose, not omniscience

A creature acts on what it can perceive and know. Use its senses as printed; ordinary hearing does not become precise location through any wall. Give players visible signs when a capability should be recognizable: a troll's closing wounds, a wolf's circling pack, or a sentinel that stops at a boundary.

The tactics line suggests useful choices. Adapt them to the scene without changing the card. A hungry animal might protect food, while one defending young risks more. A guard can retreat, surrender or negotiate while still alive. At 0 HP, an ordinary creature does not automatically receive a chance for last-minute stabilization.

Knowledge of a familiar fantasy trope can suggest an experiment, but only this creature's printed rules determine its effect. If a player tries something that would plainly fail here, offer information their hero could reasonably perceive before they spend an action on a mistaken assumption.

Summoned forms

Summons are energy shaped to resemble and act like creatures. They cannot receive healing and disappear at 0 HP without a body or permanent loot. They are still tangible: they occupy squares, block movement and can be damaged, pushed or grappled unless their own card states an exception.

A ring-and-spark marker in the upper-right corner identifies a summonable creature. Its label gives the category and minimum level: Animal 1, for example. Select the marker in the PDF to open that creature’s player profile. No marker means the creature is not an eligible summon.

Use the separate player profile for an eligible summon. Its attack outcomes run Weak to Strong attack, and its modifiers already express the player's perspective. Do not reverse the DA card mentally or import its independent Reactions. A creature is eligible only where the profile explicitly lists the relevant category and tier.

Controller spendsOne summon receives
Main ActionMain Action and Maneuver
ManeuverManeuver and movement
Summoning card's immediate free Main commandMain Action and Maneuver; this counts as that summon's command for the turn

A summon receives at most one command on its controller's turn. The controller may spend Main and Maneuver on different summons. Normal downward conversion applies; a Main-command package does not also include free movement. Convert its Maneuver to movement if it must approach before attacking.

No command means no activity: no following, watching, alerting, helping or continued attack. Existing conditions and durations still resolve on the controller's turn. Commands cannot be saved for an enemy turn. Summons have no independent Reactions, opportunity attacks or summon chains.

Keep the nearest occupied squares of controller and summon within six squares, using ordinary grid distance. Exactly six is valid; beyond six it immediately disappears. Movement of either participant, including forced movement, can break the tether. It also disappears if the controller becomes unconscious or dies.

> Example: the Moon Hart. A commanded summoned hart uses Battle Mending. Its > controller pays 3 HP before resolution, bypassing resistance and remaining above > 0. The hart does not also pay. Roll the hart's Reason and heal 5/10/15, reduced > by the eligible recipient's Life resistance, minimum 1 where HP is missing. The > hart itself cannot be healed. An ordinary unsummoned hart pays its own healing cost.

Find the next creature

The following chapter groups creatures into alphabetical families, keeping variants together. Each individual is also indexed by name, CV, habitat and role. These categories help you find candidates; they do not add abilities, summon eligibility, resistance or moral alignment.

The monster ability appendix supports preparation and adaptation. The creature card remains complete enough to run without chasing that appendix during a turn. Use the indexes to find creatures by name, CV, family, habitat or role.
